sententiae.latin: Carpe diem, quam minimum crēdula posterō.
sententiae.english: Seize the day, trusting as little as possible in tomorrow.
sententiae.note: Horace is telling a young woman, Leuconoë, to stop asking astrologers about the future. *Carpe* is really "pluck", as you pluck ripe fruit: the day is ready, so pick it.

options: Accusative: it is what is to be seized
steps.explain: *diem* is the accusative of *diēs*, the object of *carpe*. *Carpe* is a command to one person, so its subject is "you".

steps.prompt: *crēdula* is feminine. What does that tell you?
options: The person being spoken to is a woman
steps.explain: *crēdula* describes "you", the one told to seize the day. The poem is addressed to Leuconoë. *posterō* is dative: the thing she should not trust.

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *crēdulus* (from *crēdō*, "I believe")?
steps.explain: Credulous means too ready to believe. Credit, creed and incredible come from *crēdō* too. (Decrease comes from *crēscō*, "grow".)

sententiae.english: I came, I saw, I conquered.
sententiae.source: Julius Caesar, as Suetonius reports (*Divus Julius* 37)
sententiae.note: Caesar's whole account of a five-day war against King Pharnaces in 47 BC. Suetonius says the three words were carried on a placard in his triumph.

steps.prompt: What tense are all three verbs?
steps.explain: The *-ī* ending is the perfect's "I". The perfect stems often lengthen the vowel: *veniō* → *vēnī*, *videō* → *vīdī*.
The perfect endings run *-ī, -istī, -it, -imus, -istis, -ērunt*. So *vīcimus*, "we conquered".

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *vincō, vīcī, victum*?
steps.explain: Victory, victor, convince and invincible all come from *vincō*. (Vicious comes from *vitium*, "fault"; vicar from *vicis*, "turn, place".)

sententiae.english: Fortune helps the brave.
sententiae.source: Pliny the Elder, as his nephew reports (Pliny, *Letters* 6.16)
sententiae.note: Pliny's uncle says it as he steers his ships toward Vesuvius during the eruption, against the helmsman's advice. He died on the shore the next day. The course reads this letter in Level III.

steps.explain: *fortūna* is nominative singular, matching the singular verb *iuvat*. *Fortēs* is accusative plural, "the brave", the people fortune helps. The endings decide, not the order.
Latin can put the object first for emphasis: "the brave, fortune helps".

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *iuvō, iūtum*, "help", through *adiuvō*?
steps.explain: An adjutant is an officer's assistant. Aid comes from the same verb, through French. (Juvenile comes from *iuvenis*, "young"; jury from *iūrō*, "swear".)

sententiae.latin: Ōdī et amō. Quārē id faciam, fortasse requīris.
sententiae.english: I hate and I love. Why do I do it, perhaps you ask.
sententiae.note: The first line of a two-line poem. The second answers: *nesciō, sed fierī sentiō et excrucior*, "I don't know, but I feel it happening, and I am in torment."

gloss.meaning: I hate (perfect in form, present in meaning)

steps.prompt: *ōdī* looks like a perfect. What does it mean?
steps.explain: *ōdī*, like *meminī* "I remember", has only perfect forms, with a present meaning.

options: It is in an indirect question after *requīris*
steps.explain: A question reported after a verb of asking goes into the subjunctive: "you ask why I do it".

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from the same root as *ōdī*?
steps.explain: Odious, "hateful", comes from *odium*, "hatred". (Odor comes from *odor*, "smell"; ode is Greek.)

sententiae.latin: Forsan et haec ōlim meminisse iuvābit.
sententiae.english: Perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember even these things.
sententiae.note: Aeneas to his shipwrecked men after the storm. Vergil adds that he hid his own fear behind a hopeful face: *spem vultū simulat, premit altum corde dolōrem*.

gloss.meaning: it pleases, it is a joy

steps.latin: Forsan et haec ōlim meminisse iuvābit.
options: it will be a pleasure to remember
steps.explain: *iuvat* with an infinitive means "it is pleasing to...". *-bit* makes it future. *meminisse* is the infinitive of *meminī*.

options: The troubles they have just been through
steps.explain: *haec*, neuter plural, "these things": the storm, the lost ships, the hunger. *et* here means "even".
A memento is a keepsake: it is the command *mementō*, "remember!". (Member comes from *membrum*, "limb".)

sententiae.english: While I breathe, I hope.
sententiae.source: a Latin proverb; the motto of South Carolina
sententiae.note: Two verbs that sound almost alike. Cicero knew the idea: while a sick man has breath, he writes to Atticus, there is said to be hope.

steps.explain: *-ō* is the first-person singular ending of the present: *spīrō*, "I breathe"; *spērō*, "I hope".

steps.prompt: Make it "while we breathe": give the "we" form of *spīrō*.
steps.explain: *spīrō, spīrās, spīrat, spīrāmus, spīrātis, spīrant*. "While we breathe, we hope": *dum spīrāmus, spērāmus*.

steps.prompt: Which pair of English words comes from these two verbs?
steps.explain: Inspire, respiration and spirit come from *spīrō*; desperate, "out of hope", from *spērō*.

sententiae.english: Who will guard the guards themselves?
sententiae.note: In Juvenal, the guards are hired to keep a wife faithful, and they can be bribed. The line is now asked of anyone who holds power over others.

steps.explain: Fourth-conjugation futures go *-iam, -iēs, -iet*: *custōdiet*, "will guard".
*quis* is the subject. *-ēs* can be nominative or accusative plural; *ipsōs*, clearly accusative, agrees with it and settles it.
Custody and custodian: guarding and keeping. (Custom, customer and costume come from *cōnsuētūdō*, "habit".)

sententiae.latin: Sunt lacrimae rērum et mentem mortālia tangunt.
sententiae.english: There are tears for things, and mortal things touch the mind.
sententiae.note: In Carthage, Aeneas finds the Trojan War painted on the walls of Juno's temple and weeps: even here, far away, people know and grieve for it. Few lines in Latin have been argued over more.

gloss.meaning: thing, event; rērum, of or for things

steps.explain: *sunt* at the start of a sentence often means "there are". *lacrimae* is nominative plural, the subject.
*mortālia*, neuter plural, is the subject of plural *tangunt*. *mentem*, accusative singular, is what they touch.

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *tangō, tāctum*?
steps.explain: Tangible, "able to be touched". Also tact, contact, contagious and tangent. (Tangerines are named after Tangier.)

sententiae.english: Make haste slowly.
sententiae.source: the favorite saying of Augustus, as Suetonius reports (*Divus Augustus* 25)
sententiae.note: Suetonius says Augustus thought nothing less fitting in a general than haste and rashness, and was always saying this (in Greek). A dolphin wrapped round an anchor became its emblem.

steps.explain: The singular command of a first-conjugation verb is the bare stem: *festīnā*, "hurry!".

steps.prompt: What is it called when "hurry" is paired with "slowly"?
steps.explain: An oxymoron joins two ideas that seem to contradict, to make you think: act promptly, but carefully.
To relent is to slow again, to soften. (Lentil comes from *lēns*, the plant; a lens is named after the lentil, for its shape.)

sententiae.english: I fear the Greeks, even when they bring gifts.
sententiae.note: Laocoön's warning about the wooden horse. No one listens; soon after, two sea serpents kill him and his sons, and the Trojans take it as a sign he was wrong.

steps.prompt: *ferentēs* is a participle. Whom does it describe?
steps.explain: *ferentēs* is accusative plural, like *Danaōs*: "the Greeks, even (when) bringing gifts". *dōna* is its object.
Neuter plurals end in *-a* in both nominative and accusative. Here the gifts are what is carried, so accusative.
Donation, donor and condone come from *dōnum* and *dōnō*, "give". (Dome comes from *domus*, "house".)

sententiae.english: I think, therefore I am.
sententiae.note: Descartes wrote in Latin, still the shared language of scholars in the 1600s. Looking for one thing he could not doubt, he found it: to doubt is to think, and to think you must exist.

steps.explain: *sum* is "I am". With nothing after it, it means "I exist".
*sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt*.
To cogitate is to think hard. *cōgitō* is *co-* + *agitō*, "drive together": turning something over in the mind.

sententiae.latin: Tantae mōlis erat Rōmānam condere gentem.
sententiae.english: So great a labor it was to found the Roman people.
sententiae.note: The last line of the *Aeneid*'s opening. After Juno's anger and years of wandering, Vergil weighs the whole story in one line. *mōlēs* is literally a mass, a huge weight.

options: the founder of the Roman people
steps.explain: *condere* is an infinitive, "to found"; *Rōmānam ... gentem* is its object, adjective and noun wrapped around the verb, as Vergil likes.
A genitive can describe, as in "a man of great courage". With *erat*: "(it) was (a matter) of so great an effort".
A molecule is "a little mass". Demolish is another: *dēmōlior*, "pull down a mass". (Mollusc comes from *mollis*, "soft".)

sententiae.english: Skill takes long to learn; life is short.
sententiae.source: the Latin form of a saying of the Greek doctor Hippocrates
sententiae.note: Hippocrates meant medicine: the craft takes a lifetime, and life is too short for it. Seneca quotes it at the start of *On the Shortness of Life*.

steps.prompt: What verb is understood in both halves?
steps.explain: Latin often leaves out *est*: "Art (is) long, life (is) short."

steps.prompt: Why *longa* but *brevis*, if both describe feminine nouns?
options: They are different kinds of adjective, both feminine nominative singular
steps.explain: *longus, -a, -um* and *brevis, -e* belong to different adjective families. Agreement is in gender, number and case, not spelling.
Brief, brevity and abbreviate all come from *brevis*.

sententiae.latin: Ōrandum est ut sit mēns sāna in corpore sānō.
sententiae.english: You should pray for a sound mind in a sound body.
sententiae.note: Juvenal's poem is about how people pray for the wrong things: wealth, power, beauty, long life. If you must pray, he says, pray for this.

steps.explain: *in* with the ablative means "in, on". *sānō* agrees with *corpore*.

steps.prompt: What kind of clause is *ut sit mēns sāna*?
options: An indirect command: what to pray for
steps.explain: Verbs of asking, praying and ordering take *ut* + subjunctive for the thing asked: "one must pray that there be a sound mind".

steps.prompt: Type the English word from *sānus* meaning "of sound mind".
steps.explain: Sane, sanity, insane and sanitary all come from *sānus*, "healthy".

sententiae.latin: Sed fugit intereā, fugit irreparābile tempus.
sententiae.english: But meanwhile it flies, time flies beyond recall.
sententiae.note: The source of "time flies", *tempus fugit*. In a poem on farming, Vergil breaks off a long passage on horses and cattle: he has lingered too long, and time is going.

steps.prompt: What is the subject of both verbs?
steps.latin: Sed fugit intereā, fugit irreparābile tempus.
steps.explain: *tempus*, neuter nominative, is held back to the end of the line. *irreparābile* agrees with it.

options: It stresses how time keeps slipping away
steps.explain: Repeating a word at the start of each phrase (anaphora) presses the point, as if time were running on while he speaks.

steps.prompt: Type an English word from *fugiō* for someone on the run from the law.
steps.explain: A fugitive (*fugitīvus*) is one who flees. Refuge, "a place to flee back to", comes from it too.

sententiae.latin: Nūllus est liber tam malus ut nōn aliquā parte prōsit.
sententiae.english: No book is so bad that it is not useful in some part.
sententiae.source: Pliny the Elder's saying, as his nephew reports (Pliny, *Letters* 3.5)
sententiae.note: Pliny's uncle read constantly, taking notes at dinner and on journeys; he left 160 notebooks of extracts. His nephew reports the saying in indirect speech; this is the form it is usually quoted in.

steps.prompt: What kind of clause is *ut nōn aliquā parte prōsit*?
steps.latin: tam malus ut nōn aliquā parte prōsit
options: Purpose: "so as not to be useful"
Result: "so bad that it is not useful"
steps.explain: *tam*, "so", signals a result clause: *ut* + subjunctive, and "not" is *ut nōn*. A purpose clause would say *nē*.
An ablative with no preposition, saying in what respect: "useful in some part".

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *liber, librī*?
steps.explain: A library holds *librī*. (Liberty comes from a different word, *līber* with a long *ī*, "free".)

sententiae.latin: Omnia vincit Amor: et nōs cēdāmus Amōrī.
sententiae.english: Love conquers all things: let us too give way to Love.
sententiae.note: The poet Gallus, sick with love, gives up the fight at the end of Vergil's last Eclogue. *Amor* is the god as well as the feeling, hence the capital.

steps.explain: Neuter plural *omnia* could be nominative or accusative. *Amor* is the singular subject of *vincit*, so *omnia* is the object.
A first-person subjunctive standing on its own urges: "let us...". This is the hortatory subjunctive.

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *cēdō*, "go, give way"?
steps.explain: Concede, recede, precede, proceed and exceed all come from *cēdō*. (Decide comes from *caedō*, "cut".)

sententiae.english: Oh, the times! Oh, the ways of men!
sententiae.note: Cicero, consul in 63 BC, before the senate: Catiline is plotting against the state, and still sits among them. He goes on, *senātus haec intellegit, cōnsul videt; hic tamen vīvit*.

gloss.meaning: custom; in the plural, character, morals

steps.explain: Neuter *tempus* has a plural in *-a*: *tempora*. *mōs, mōris* becomes *mōrēs*.

options: the ways and morals of the age
steps.explain: *mōs* is a custom; in the plural, the ways people live. Cicero laments how far things have fallen. (*morae* would be "delays".)

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *mōs, mōris*?
steps.explain: Moral and morale come from *mōs*. (A moratorium is a delay, from *mora*; mortal comes from *mors*, "death".)

sententiae.english: A drop hollows out stone.
sententiae.note: Ovid, in exile on the Black Sea, lists what time wears away: a drop hollows stone, a ring thins with use. Only his sorrow, he says, does not wear away.

steps.explain: *lapidem* is the accusative of *lapis*: what the drop hollows. *gutta* is nominative, the subject.
Subject, verb, object, in the same order as the Latin this time.
To excavate is to hollow out, *ex-* + *cavō*. Cave and cavity come from *cavus*, "hollow". (Cavalry comes from *caballus*, "horse".)

sententiae.latin: Quō ūsque tandem abūtēre, Catilīna, patientiā nostrā?
sententiae.english: How long, Catiline, will you go on abusing our patience?
sententiae.note: The first words of Cicero's first speech against Catiline, the most famous opening in Latin oratory. Catiline was sitting in the senate as Cicero spoke.

steps.prompt: *abūtēre* is a form of the deponent *abūtor*. What is it?
steps.explain: *-ēre* is another spelling of *-ēris*, the second-person singular future of a third-conjugation deponent: *abūtēris* or *abūtēre*.
*ūtor* and its compound *abūtor*, with *fruor, fungor, potior* and *vēscor*, take the ablative.
He is addressed directly. A first-declension vocative looks like the nominative.

sententiae.latin: Homō sum: hūmānī nīl ā mē aliēnum putō.
sententiae.english: I am human: I think nothing human is foreign to me.
sententiae.note: In the comedy a nosy neighbor, Chremes, says it to excuse prying into another man's troubles. It became a motto for human sympathy.

steps.latin: hūmānī nīl ā mē aliēnum putō
steps.explain: A genitive after *nīl*, "nothing of the human". English says "nothing human".

steps.prompt: *putō* has an object and a word saying what it is thought to be. Which pair?
steps.explain: Verbs of thinking and calling can take an object and a predicate: "I consider nothing (to be) foreign".
Alien and alienate: belonging to another, *alius*. (Ally comes from *alligō*, "bind to"; allergy is Greek.)

sententiae.english: Let the welfare of the people be the highest law.
sententiae.note: From the law code Cicero imagines for an ideal state, describing the duty of consuls. It is the motto of Missouri.

gloss.meaning: let it be, it shall be

options: A future command: "let it be", the style of laws
steps.explain: The future imperative (*estō*, plural *suntō*) is used in laws and solemn instructions: "X shall be...".
The welfare *of* the people. *populī* could be nominative plural in form, but the sense needs "of".

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *lēx, lēgis*?
steps.explain: Legal, legislate and legitimate come from *lēx*. (Legend comes from *legō*, "read"; legion from *legiō*, a body of "chosen" men.)

sententiae.latin: Rāra avis in terrīs nigrōque simillima cycnō.
sententiae.english: A rare bird on earth, very like a black swan.
sententiae.note: Juvenal's joke about the perfect wife: as rare as a black swan, a bird Romans took to be imaginary. Europeans first saw black swans in Australia in 1697.

steps.explain: *similis*, "like", takes the dative: "very like to a black swan".

options: Joins it to what comes before: "and"
steps.explain: *-que* on a word means "and" before it: *nigrōque* = *et nigrō*.
Aviation, aviary and aviator: all birds. (Avenue comes from *adveniō*, "come to"; avid from *avidus*, "greedy".)

sententiae.english: We learn not for life but for school.
sententiae.note: A complaint, not a motto: Seneca grumbles that philosophers waste their time on clever puzzles. Schools later turned it round: *nōn scholae sed vītae discimus*.

steps.explain: *-ae* can be genitive or dative singular, or nominative plural. The sense decides: we learn *for* school.
*discō, discis, discit, discimus, discitis, discunt*: third conjugation.
A disciple, *discipulus*, is a learner; discipline is the training. (Discuss comes from *discutiō*, "shake apart".)

sententiae.english: The die is cast.
sententiae.source: Julius Caesar at the Rubicon, 49 BC, as Suetonius reports (*Divus Julius* 32)
sententiae.note: Crossing the Rubicon, the stream between his province and Italy, with an army meant civil war. A thrown die cannot be taken back.

gloss.meaning: a die; a game of dice

steps.prompt: *iacta est* is a perfect passive. What does it mean?
steps.explain: Perfect passive = perfect participle + a form of *sum*. *iacta* is feminine to agree with *ālea*.
The die, *ālea*, is what has been thrown. The verb comes first for emphasis.
Eject, reject, project, inject: each a kind of throw. In compounds *iactum* becomes *-iectum*. (Jest comes from *gesta*, "deeds".)

sententiae.english: For laws fall silent in time of war.
sententiae.note: Cicero defends Milo, whose men killed his enemy Clodius in a brawl on the Appian Way. The argument: killing in self-defense can be lawful.

steps.explain: *lēgēs*, nominative plural, with the plural verb *silent*. *arma* is accusative, after *inter*.
*inter* + accusative, "among". "Among weapons" means when the weapons are out: in war.
Silence and silent. (Silhouette is named after a French finance minister; silly is Old English.)

sententiae.english: This is my love, this my homeland.
sententiae.note: Aeneas to Dido: his heart is set on Italy, where the gods are sending him, not on Carthage. Dido, who loves him, hears it as betrayal.

options: Each agrees in gender with its noun
steps.explain: *amor* is masculine, so *hic*; *patria* is feminine, so *haec*. (*hic* here is "this", not the adverb "here".)

steps.prompt: The same word begins both phrases. What is that called?
steps.explain: Anaphora repeats a word at the start of successive phrases, for emphasis: Italy, and only Italy.
Amorous, "in love", and enamored. (Amoral is Greek *a-*, "not", + moral; amortize comes from *mors*, "death": paying a debt down to nothing.)

sententiae.english: I shall not wholly die.
sententiae.note: Horace ends his first three books of odes claiming he has built a monument more lasting than bronze. His poems will keep part of him alive, and they have.

steps.explain: *morior* is a deponent of the *capiō* type, with a future in *-iar, -iēris, -iētur*. (The present subjunctive looks the same; here the sense is future.)
*omnis* is nominative with the subject "I": not all of me will die.

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *morior, mortuus*?
steps.explain: Mortuary, mortal and mortgage (a "dead pledge") come from *morior* and *mors*.

sententiae.english: Woe to the conquered!
sententiae.note: The Gauls captured Rome around 390 BC and agreed to leave for a thousand pounds of gold. When the Romans complained the weights were rigged, the Gallic chief Brennus threw his sword onto the scale and said this.

steps.explain: *vae* takes the dative of the people the woe falls on. *-īs* can be dative or ablative plural; here it is dative.

steps.prompt: *victīs* is a participle used as a noun. Who are they?
steps.explain: *victus*, "having been conquered"; as a noun, "those who have been conquered".
*vincō, vincere, vīcī, victum*. *vīcī*, "I conquered", as in *vēnī, vīdī, vīcī*. *vincī* is "to be conquered".

sententiae.latin: Dulce et decōrum est prō patriā morī.
sententiae.english: It is sweet and fitting to die for one's country.
sententiae.note: Horace's line became a patriotic motto. In 1917 the soldier-poet Wilfred Owen, writing from the trenches, called it "the old Lie".

gloss.meaning: for, on behalf of (with the ablative)

steps.latin: Dulce et decōrum est prō patriā morī.
steps.explain: An infinitive can be a subject: "To die for one's country is sweet and fitting." The adjectives are neuter because an infinitive counts as neuter.

steps.prompt: *morī* is the infinitive of a deponent verb. What does it mean?
steps.explain: Deponents look passive but mean something active: *morior*, "I die"; *morī*, "to die".
A patriot loves the *patria*, which comes from *pater*, "father". (Patient comes from *patior*, "suffer".)

sententiae.english: Where they make a desert, they call it peace.
sententiae.note: Tacitus gives this speech to Calgacus, a chief in Scotland, before a battle against the Romans. It is a Roman writing about Rome, in the mouth of an enemy.

steps.explain: Calgacus is describing the Romans: they plunder and slaughter, and call it empire.
*appellant*, "they call", has an understood object (the desert they made) and *pācem*, the name they give it.

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *pāx, pācis*?
steps.explain: To pacify is to make peace (*pāx* + *faciō*). Also pacifist, and the Pacific, the "peaceful" ocean. (Pace comes from *passus*, "step".)

sententiae.latin: Aequam mementō rēbus in arduīs servāre mentem.
sententiae.english: Remember to keep a level head when times are hard.
sententiae.note: Horace to his friend Dellius: stay calm when things are bad, and don't get carried away when they are good, since death comes to everyone alike.

steps.latin: Aequam mementō rēbus in arduīs servāre mentem.
steps.explain: Both are feminine accusative singular. Horace wraps the whole sentence between them.
*in* + ablative, with the preposition tucked between noun and adjective, as poets often do.
Equanimity is a level mind: exactly Horace's advice. Equal, equation and equator come from *aequus* too. (Equine comes from *equus*, "horse".)

sententiae.english: This is the way to the stars.
sententiae.note: Apollo says it to Aeneas's young son Ascanius after the boy kills his first enemy: this is how one reaches undying fame.

gloss.meaning: go; itur, there is going, one goes

steps.prompt: *itur* is a passive of *eō* with no subject. Literally...
steps.explain: Latin can make a verb like "go" passive with no subject: *itur*, "there is a going". *pugnātum est*, "there was fighting", works the same way.
*ad*, "to, toward", takes the accusative. Neuter plural *astra*.
A disaster is "an ill star", *dis-* + *astrum*, from the belief that misfortune was written in the stars. (Dismal comes from *diēs malī*, "evil days".)

sententiae.latin: Historia vērō testis temporum, lūx vēritātis, vīta memoriae, magistra vītae.
sententiae.english: History, truly, is the witness of the ages, the light of truth, the life of memory, the teacher of life.
sententiae.note: In a dialogue about the ideal speaker, Cicero asks whose voice but the orator's can make history live. *Historia magistra vītae* became a slogan.

steps.prompt: What case is the second word of each pair (*temporum, vēritātis, memoriae, vītae*)?
steps.latin: testis temporum, lūx vēritātis, vīta memoriae, magistra vītae
steps.explain: Four pairs, each a noun and a genitive: witness *of* the ages, light *of* truth. The pattern tells you *vītae* is genitive too.
A noun describing a feminine noun takes its feminine form when it has one: history is a woman teacher.
To testify is to act as a witness. Testament, protest and contest share the root. (Text comes from *texō*, "weave".)

sententiae.english: Everything changes; nothing dies.
sententiae.note: The philosopher Pythagoras speaks in the last book of the *Metamorphoses*, a poem entirely about change. The soul, he says, only moves from body to body.

steps.explain: *-ntur* is the third-person plural passive: "are changed". English often just says "change".
*inter* + *it*: like *it*, "goes", it is present tense. Compare *pereō*, "go through, perish".
A mutation is a change; commute and permutation too. (Mute comes from *mūtus*, "silent"; mutiny from *moveō*.)

sententiae.english: Furthermore, I think Carthage must be destroyed.
sententiae.source: Cato the Elder, as tradition reports
sententiae.note: Plutarch says Cato ended every speech in the senate, on any subject, by saying Carthage must be destroyed. The Latin wording is later, the habit ancient. Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC.

steps.explain: After *cēnseō*, "I think", the thought goes into accusative + infinitive: Carthage (accusative) to be destroyed (infinitive).
The gerundive with *sum* says what must be done (the passive periphrastic). *dēlendam* is feminine accusative to agree with *Carthāginem*.

steps.prompt: Type the English word from *dēleō, dēlētum* for removing text.
steps.explain: Delete comes from *dēlētum*. Indelible, "that cannot be wiped out", too.

sententiae.english: I have finished a monument more lasting than bronze.
sententiae.note: The first line of the same poem as *nōn omnis moriar*. His poems, Horace says, will outlast bronze statues and the pyramids.

steps.explain: After a comparative, the ablative can mean "than": *aere perennius*. The other way is *quam aes*.
Comparatives end in *-ior* (masculine and feminine) and *-ius* (neuter).
A perennial plant comes back year after year: *per* + *annus*, "through the years".

sententiae.latin: Nōn ignāra malī miserīs succurrere discō.
sententiae.english: No stranger to trouble myself, I am learning to help those in need.
sententiae.note: Dido welcomes the shipwrecked Trojans to Carthage. She was once a refugee herself, fleeing her brother across the sea.

steps.prompt: *Nōn ignāra* is litotes. What does it mean?
steps.latin: Nōn ignāra malī miserīs succurrere discō.
steps.explain: Litotes says something by denying its opposite: "not unacquainted" means "all too familiar".
The subject of *discō* is Dido, so the adjective describing her is feminine nominative.
Verbs of helping, like *succurrō* and *subveniō*, take the dative: run to help *for* the wretched.

sententiae.latin: Duās tantum rēs anxius optat, pānem et circēnsēs.
sententiae.english: It anxiously wants two things only: bread and circuses.
sententiae.note: Juvenal on the Roman people: once they handed out commands and armies at elections; now they want only free grain and the chariot races.

gloss.meaning: games in the Circus, the races

steps.explain: *duās* is the feminine accusative of *duo*, agreeing with *rēs*. *pānem et circēnsēs*, also accusative, name the two things.
A companion is someone you share bread with: *com-*, "with", + *pānis*. (Panic comes from the Greek god Pan.)

sententiae.latin: Ūna salūs victīs nūllam spērāre salūtem.
sententiae.english: The one safety for the conquered is to hope for no safety.
sententiae.note: Aeneas rallies his last companions on the night Troy falls: the city is lost, so they should rush into the fighting and die well.

steps.prompt: *salūs ... salūtem*: the same word in two cases. What is that called?
steps.latin: Ūna salūs victīs nūllam spērāre salūtem.
steps.explain: Polyptoton repeats a word in a different form: nominative *salūs*, accusative *salūtem*. It sharpens the paradox.

steps.prompt: What is the subject of the understood *est*?
steps.explain: "The one safety ... (is) to hope for none": *Ūna salūs* is the subject; the infinitive phrase says what it is.
To salute someone was to wish them *salūs*, health. (Salary comes from *sāl*, "salt".)

sententiae.latin: Tū regere imperiō populōs, Rōmāne, mementō.
sententiae.english: You, Roman, remember to rule the nations with your power.
sententiae.note: In the underworld, Anchises tells Aeneas what Rome's art will be. Others may cast bronze and chart the stars better; Rome's is to rule, to spare the conquered and war down the proud.

steps.latin: Tū regere imperiō populōs, Rōmāne, mementō.
steps.explain: Second-declension *-us* nouns have a vocative in *-e*. Anchises speaks to every Roman to come.
An ablative of means, with no preposition: rule *by* command.
*mementō* takes an infinitive. Vergil saves the command for the end of the line.

sententiae.english: The way down to Avernus is easy.
sententiae.note: The Sibyl warns Aeneas: going down to the underworld is easy, its door stands open night and day. Coming back is the hard part: *hoc opus, hic labor est*.

gloss.meaning: a lake near Naples, a way into the underworld

steps.explain: As in many sayings, *est* is left out: "the descent (is) easy".

steps.prompt: *Avernō* is dative. What does it mean here?
steps.explain: Poets use the dative for the place someone goes to: "the way down to Avernus".
Facility and facilitate: making things easy. (Face comes from *faciēs*; fascinate from *fascinō*, "bewitch".)

sententiae.latin: Quid nōn mortālia pectora cōgis, aurī sacra famēs!
sententiae.english: What do you not drive human hearts to, accursed hunger for gold!
sententiae.note: Aeneas tells how the king of Thrace murdered Priam's youngest son, Polydorus, for the gold sent with him for safekeeping. *sacer* can mean "holy" or "accursed".

steps.latin: Quid nōn mortālia pectora cōgis, aurī sacra famēs!
options: *aurī sacra famēs*, the hunger for gold
steps.explain: Apostrophe: Aeneas turns to speak to an abstraction, greed for gold, as if it could hear.
An objective genitive: gold is what the hunger is for.
Famine and famished come from *famēs*. (Fame and famous come from *fāma*, "report"; family from *familia*.)

sententiae.english: Relentless work overcame everything.
sententiae.note: After the Golden Age, Vergil says, Jupiter made life hard so that people would have to invent: work, not ease, built the arts. *Labor omnia vincit* is the motto of Oklahoma.

steps.explain: *improbus* is masculine nominative singular, like *labor*. In Vergil it starts the next line, which makes it land harder.
*vincō, vincere, vīcī*: *vīcit* is the perfect, "overcame, has overcome".
A laboratory is a place of work; elaborate and collaborate too. (Labyrinth is Greek.)

sententiae.latin: Nīl dēspērandum Teucrō duce et auspice Teucrō.
sententiae.english: There is no need to despair with Teucer as leader and Teucer as guide.
sententiae.note: The hero Teucer, exiled by his father, cheers his men before sailing to found a new city. Horace tells the story to urge a friend to drown his cares in wine.

steps.prompt: *Teucrō duce* is an ablative absolute with no participle. How does it go into English?
steps.explain: Two nouns in the ablative, with "being" understood: "Teucer (being) leader". Latin has no present participle of *sum*.
The gerundive says what must (or here, need not) be done: "nothing is to be despaired of".

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *dux, ducis*?
steps.explain: A duke is a leader. Conduct, educate and produce come from *dūcō*, "lead".

sententiae.english: He whom the gods love dies young.
sententiae.note: In Plautus it is a joke: a slave says it of a foolish old man, meaning the gods must hate him, since he is still alive. Later readers took it seriously.

steps.explain: Inside its own clause, *quem* is the object of *dīligunt*. The "he" it refers to is left out; he is the subject of *moritur*.
*deus* has a short plural: *dī* (or *deī*), "gods", the subject of *dīligunt*.
An adolescent is "growing up", *adolēscō*. Adult, "grown up", is its perfect participle.

sententiae.english: To spare the conquered and to war down the proud.
sententiae.note: The end of Anchises' charge to Rome. Readers still argue whether Aeneas lives up to it when he kills Turnus in the poem's last lines.

steps.explain: Verbs of sparing, pleasing, helping and trusting often take the dative.
*-ōs* is the second-declension accusative plural: the proud are the ones warred down.
Superb: splendid. *superbus* itself grows from *super*, "above": the proud hold themselves above others.

sententiae.english: I sing of arms and the man.
sententiae.note: The first words of the *Aeneid*. "Arms" are the wars in Italy of the second half; "the man" is Aeneas, whose wanderings fill the first. Homer began the *Odyssey* with "the man" and the *Iliad* with war: Vergil takes on both at once.

options: Accusative: what the poet sings of
steps.explain: *canō* takes a direct object: "I sing arms and the man". *arma* is neuter plural, *virum* masculine singular, both accusative.
*-que* joins its word to the one before it: *arma virumque* = *arma et virum*.
Army, armor, armada and disarm come from *arma*. (The arm of the body is Old English; harmony is Greek.)

sententiae.latin: Dīmidium factī quī coepit habet: sapere audē.
sententiae.english: Well begun is half done: dare to be wise.
sententiae.note: Horace to a young friend: stop putting off the good life like a man waiting for a river to finish flowing past. Kant took *sapere aude* as the motto of the Enlightenment.

options: *quī coepit*: the one who has begun
steps.explain: The relative clause stands for its own antecedent: "(he) who has begun has half the task". *dīmidium* is the object.
Second-conjugation commands end in *-ē*: *audē*, "dare!". *sapere* is the infinitive it takes: "dare to be wise".

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *sapiō*, "be wise"?
steps.explain: Sapient means wise, and *Homo sapiens* is "wise man". Savant and savvy come from the same verb through French and Portuguese.

sententiae.latin: Omnia aliēna sunt, tempus tantum nostrum est.
sententiae.english: Everything else belongs to others; only time is ours.
sententiae.note: From the first of Seneca's letters to his friend Lucilius, which begins "claim yourself for yourself" and argues that time is the one possession we let others steal.

steps.explain: *omnia*, "all things", is neuter plural, so the adjective is too: *aliēna*.
*tantum* as an adverb means "only": "time alone is ours". As an adjective, *tantus*, it means "so great".

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *tempus, temporis*?
steps.explain: Temporary and contemporary come from *tempus*. (Temple the building is *templum*; tempt is *temptō*.)

sententiae.english: Who benefits?
sententiae.source: Cicero, *For Roscius of Ameria* 84, quoting the judge Lucius Cassius
sententiae.note: Cassius, a famously strict judge, always asked whom a crime would profit. Cicero turns the question on the men accusing his client of murdering his own father.

gloss.meaning: who? what?; cui, to or for whom

steps.explain: *cui* is the dative of *quis*: "to whom, for whom".

steps.prompt: *bonō* is a dative of purpose. Together, *cui bonō* is literally...
steps.explain: A "double dative": one for the person (*cui*), one for the purpose (*bonō*). Latin says the thing "is for a benefit to" someone.
A bonus is "a good thing" extra. Bounty and bonanza come from *bonus* too.

sententiae.english: Let us live, my Lesbia, and let us love.
sententiae.note: The poem goes on to ask for a thousand kisses, then a hundred, then another thousand, and to mix up the count so no envious person can know the total.

steps.prompt: *vīvāmus* and *amēmus* are subjunctives. What do they do?
steps.explain: The hortatory subjunctive, first person plural: "let us...". *vīvāmus* is from *vīvō* (third conjugation), *amēmus* from *amō* (first).
She is addressed directly. A first-declension vocative looks like the nominative; *mea* agrees with it.
Vivid, revive and survive come from *vīvō*. (Visit comes from *vīsō*; vinyl from *vīnum*, "wine".)

sententiae.english: As many people, so many opinions.
sententiae.note: In the comedy a young man asks three lawyers for advice and gets three different answers. The line is the joke, and the name of this feature: a *sententia* is an opinion, and a pithy saying.

steps.explain: Latin leaves out *sunt*: "(there are) as many opinions as (there are) people".

steps.prompt: *quot ... tot* work as a pair. Which English pair is closest?
steps.explain: Correlatives: *quot* "as many as" and *tot* "so many", like *tālis ... quālis*, "such ... as".
A sentence is a complete thought, and a judge's sentence is an opinion, from *sententia*. Sentiment comes from the same verb, *sentiō*.

sententiae.english: Let them hate, so long as they fear.
sententiae.source: the poet Accius; Suetonius says Caligula was always quoting it (*Caligula* 30)
sententiae.note: A line spoken by the tyrant Atreus in a lost tragedy by Accius. Cicero quotes it as the creed of tyrants, and Suetonius as the emperor Caligula's favorite saying.

gloss.meaning: here, so long as, provided that

steps.prompt: *ōderint* is a perfect subjunctive of *ōdī*. How is it used?
options: As a command or wish: "let them hate"
steps.explain: A jussive subjunctive, third person: "let them...". *ōdī* has only perfect forms, so its subjunctive is perfect in form, present in sense.
*dum* (or *dummodo*) + subjunctive states a condition: "provided they fear".
Odium, "general hatred", and odious are both from *ōdī*.

sententiae.english: Is there such great anger in the minds of the gods?
sententiae.note: The poet's own question at the end of the invocation to the Muse: why should Juno hound a man so good? The *Aeneid* never quite answers it.

options: Makes the sentence a yes-or-no question
steps.explain: *-ne* on the first word asks a question: "(are there) such angers...?".

options: Dative of possession: "belonging to heavenly minds"
steps.explain: With *sunt* (understood), the dative names the owner: "are there such angers to heavenly minds?", i.e. do the gods have them.
Celestial, "heavenly", from *caelum*, "sky". (Celebrate comes from *celeber*, "crowded"; cellar from *cella*, "storeroom".)

sententiae.english: This is the task, this the toil.
sententiae.note: The Sibyl to Aeneas, just after *facilis dēscēnsus Avernō*: going down to the dead is easy; coming back up to the light, that is the work.

steps.explain: The demonstrative agrees with its noun: *hoc opus* (neuter), *hic labor* (masculine).

steps.prompt: The two phrases have the same shape. What is that called?
steps.explain: Two short phrases built alike, each starting with a form of *hic*: the repetition drives the point home.

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *opus, operis*?
steps.explain: An opera is a "work", and so is an opus. Operate and cooperate come from *operor*, from the same root.

sententiae.latin: Iam seges est ubi Trōia fuit.
sententiae.english: Now there is a field of grain where Troy once stood.
sententiae.note: Penelope writes to Ulysses: Troy fell years ago, its site is farmland, and still he has not come home.

steps.prompt: What tense is *fuit*, and why here?
steps.latin: Iam seges est ubi Trōia fuit.
options: Perfect: Troy was, and is no more
steps.explain: *fuit*, "was, has been": the perfect sets a finished past against the present *est*.

steps.prompt: What does *est* mean at the start of this sentence?
steps.explain: *est* with a subject after it often means "there is": "there is now grain".

steps.prompt: The line sets present and past side by side. What is the effect?
options: Time has passed and Troy is gone, yet he is still away
The war is still going on
steps.explain: The contrast *est ... fuit* compresses the whole war into one line: Penelope's waiting has outlasted a city.

sententiae.english: I see the better way and approve it; I follow the worse.
sententiae.note: Medea, falling in love with Jason, knows she should not help him betray her father, and knows she will. A famous line about knowing the good and not doing it.

steps.explain: The comparative of *bonus* is *melior, melius*; the neuter plural *meliōra* means "better things".

steps.prompt: *sequor* looks passive. What does it mean?
steps.explain: Deponent verbs have passive forms with active meanings: *sequor*, "I follow".

steps.prompt: The two halves oppose *meliōra* and *dēteriōra*. What is that called?
steps.explain: Antithesis sets opposites against each other in matching positions: better/worse, see-and-approve/follow.

sententiae.latin: Et facere et patī fortia Rōmānum est.
sententiae.english: To do and to suffer brave things is the Roman way.
sententiae.note: Mucius Scaevola, captured trying to kill the Etruscan king Porsenna, thrusts his right hand into a fire to show how little he cares for pain. Porsenna, impressed, lets him go.

steps.latin: Et facere et patī fortia Rōmānum est.
steps.explain: "To do and to suffer brave things is Roman": the infinitives are the subject, *fortia* their object.

options: It describes the infinitives, which count as neuter
It is a noun: "the Roman man"
steps.explain: A predicate adjective describing an infinitive is neuter singular: "(is) a Roman thing".

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *patior, passus*?
steps.explain: Patient and passion come from *patior*, "suffer". (Paternal comes from *pater*.)

sententiae.latin: Vincere scīs, Hannibal; victōriā ūtī nescīs.
sententiae.english: You know how to win, Hannibal; you do not know how to use a victory.
sententiae.source: Maharbal to Hannibal after Cannae, as Livy reports (22.51)
sententiae.note: After the great Carthaginian victory at Cannae in 216 BC, the cavalry commander Maharbal urged Hannibal to march on Rome at once. Hannibal waited, and Rome survived.

steps.explain: *ūtor, fruor, fungor, potior* and *vēscor* take the ablative: "to make use of a victory".

steps.prompt: The two halves set *scīs* against *nescīs*. What is that called?
steps.explain: Opposites in matching places: you know / you do not know.
Science is knowledge; conscious and omniscient come from *sciō* too.

sententiae.english: Without anger or favor.
sententiae.note: Tacitus promises to write the history of the emperors without anger or partisanship, since he has no reason for either. Whether he kept the promise is still argued.

steps.explain: *sine* always takes the ablative.
*studium* is keenness for something or someone; of a historian, taking sides.
Irate and ire, "anger". (Irony is Greek; irrigate comes from *rigō*, "water".)

sententiae.english: Friends, I have lost a day.
sententiae.source: the emperor Titus, as Suetonius reports (*Titus* 8)
sententiae.note: Titus, Suetonius says, remembered at dinner one evening that he had done no one a favor all day, and said this. Suetonius calls it a remark worth remembering.

steps.explain: Titus is speaking to his friends. The vocative plural of the second declension looks like the nominative plural.
*perdō, perdere, perdidī*: the perfect, first person singular.

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *perdō*, "destroy, lose"?
steps.explain: Perdition is ruin, being lost. (Pardon is from *dōnō*, "give".)

sententiae.english: What an artist dies in me!
sententiae.source: the emperor Nero, as Suetonius reports (*Nero* 49)
sententiae.note: Nero's last words, Suetonius says, repeated as he prepared to kill himself in 68 AD: the emperor who fancied himself a singer and actor mourned the performer more than the ruler.

steps.explain: *pereō* is a compound of *eō*, "go": *per-eō*, "go through, perish", first person singular.

options: It describes the subject, "I": "as what an artist I die"
steps.explain: A predicate nominative with an intransitive verb: "I die (as) what an artist!".
Artifice and artificial: something made by art. (Article is from *artus*, "joint".)

sententiae.english: Each day is the pupil of the one before.
sententiae.note: Publilius, a freed slave from Syria, wrote mimes for the Roman stage in Caesar's time. What survives is a collection of about 700 one-line sayings, in alphabetical order.

steps.explain: *diēs* with its adjective *posterior* is the subject; *discipulus* is what it is, and *priōris* (genitive) says whose.
*prior, priōris*: the genitive singular. *diēī* is understood with it.
A disciple is a learner; discipline is a learner's training.

sententiae.english: Fools fear fortune; the wise bear it.
sententiae.note: A Stoic idea in a single line: what happens to us is not in our power, but how we take it is.

steps.explain: Latin often gives an object once and lets it serve both verbs: the wise bear (fortune).

steps.prompt: Adjectives like *stultī* and *sapientēs* are used here as...
steps.explain: A masculine plural adjective on its own means people of that kind.

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *ferō*, "bear, carry"?
steps.explain: Transfer, refer, confer and infer are all compounds of *ferō*. (Fertile comes from *ferāx*, related, but not the verb itself.)

sententiae.english: People learn while they teach.
sententiae.note: Seneca advises Lucilius to spend time with those who can make him better, and with those he can make better himself, since teaching teaches the teacher. Hence the proverb *docendō discimus*.

steps.explain: *dum* meaning "while" takes the present indicative, even of past time.
The long *-ē-* of *docēre* marks the second conjugation; *discō, discere* is third.
A doctor was first a teacher; doctrine, document and docile come from *doceō* too.

sententiae.latin: Nōn est ad astra mollis ē terrīs via.
sententiae.english: There is no easy road from the earth to the stars.
sententiae.note: From Seneca's tragedy of Hercules, who earned his place among the gods through twelve labors. Compare Vergil's *sīc itur ad astra*.

steps.latin: Nōn est ad astra mollis ē terrīs via.
steps.explain: *mollis* is feminine nominative singular, like *via*, which comes at the very end.
*ē/ex* takes the ablative: "from the lands".
To mollify is to soften. Mollusc, a soft-bodied animal, too.

sententiae.latin: Fās est et ab hoste docērī.
sententiae.english: It is right to learn even from an enemy.
sententiae.note: Juno, watching Bacchus drive his enemies mad, decides to use the same weapon herself: if madness works for him, she can learn from it.

steps.latin: Fās est et ab hoste docērī.
options: A present passive infinitive: "to be taught"
steps.explain: Second-conjugation passive infinitives end in *-ērī*: *docērī*, "to be taught".

options: The person by whom something is done: ablative of agent
steps.explain: With a passive verb, *ā/ab* + ablative names the agent: "taught by an enemy".
Hostile means like an enemy. (Hostel comes from *hospes*, "guest"; hostage from *obses* through French.)

sententiae.latin: Dōnec eris fēlīx, multōs numerābis amīcōs.
sententiae.english: As long as you are lucky, you will count many friends.
sententiae.note: The next line finishes the thought: *tempora sī fuerint nūbila, sōlus eris*, "if the times turn cloudy, you will be alone." Ovid wrote it in exile, when many friends had gone quiet.

steps.latin: Dōnec eris fēlīx, multōs numerābis amīcōs.
steps.explain: *eris* is the future of *sum*, "you will be"; *-bis* makes the first-conjugation future *numerābis*, "you will count".

steps.prompt: *multōs* is separated from *amīcōs*. What does it agree with?
steps.explain: Poets spread adjective and noun across the line; the endings keep them together.
Felicity is happiness; felicitous means apt. (Feline comes from *fēlēs*, "cat".)

sententiae.english: So well does art lie hidden by its own art.
sententiae.note: Pygmalion's ivory statue looks so alive that its art is invisible. Soon after, Venus brings it to life. The idea became the proverb "the art is to hide the art".

gloss.meaning: so much, to such a degree

options: Ablative of means: "by its own art"
steps.explain: *arte suā*: the ablative of means, with no preposition.

steps.prompt: *Ars ... arte* repeats one word in two cases. What is that called?
steps.explain: Polyptoton: the same word in different forms, here nominative and ablative. It fits the paradox of art hiding art.
Latent means present but hidden. (Lateral is from *latus*, "side"; latitude from *lātus*, "wide".)

sententiae.english: There is a god within us.
sententiae.note: Ovid on poetic inspiration: when a god stirs within, we grow warm and write. The *Fasti* is his poem on the Roman calendar, month by month.

steps.explain: *in* + ablative means "in, on"; *in* + accusative would mean "into".

steps.prompt: What does *est* mean at the start?
steps.explain: A sentence opening with *est* often means "there is".
A deity is a god; divine comes from the related *dīvus*.

sententiae.english: Mind moves the mass.
sententiae.note: In the underworld Anchises explains the universe to Aeneas: a spirit within feeds heaven, earth and sea, and a mind spread through the limbs moves the whole mass.

steps.explain: *mōlem* is the accusative of *mōlēs*: the mass that the mind moves.
The *-ā-* of *agitāre* marks the first conjugation; *agitat* is its third person singular.
To agitate is to stir up. *agitō* means "keep driving", from *agō*, which gives agent and agile. (Agony is Greek; aggravate comes from *gravis*.)

sententiae.english: They can, because they think they can.
sententiae.note: In the boat race at the funeral games for Anchises, one crew is sure of winning and rows the harder for it. A motto for any race since.

options: they are seen by the enemy
steps.explain: The passive of *videō* often means "seem": "they can because they seem able".
*possum, posse, potuī*: *posse* is "to be able", completing *videntur*.
Possible and potent come from *possum* and its root *pot-*. (Post, poster and posture come from *pōnō*, "put".)

sententiae.english: A woman was the leader of the deed.
sententiae.note: Venus tells Aeneas how Dido, whose brother murdered her husband, gathered those who hated the tyrant, seized his ships and his gold, and sailed to found Carthage. Three words for the whole story.

steps.explain: Vergil drops the verb: "a woman (was) leader of the deed". The compression gives it force.
*factum, factī*: the genitive depends on *dux*, "leader of the deed".
Feminine and feminist come from *fēmina*. (Fence is short for defence; ferment comes from *fervēre*, "boil".)

sententiae.english: I recognize the traces of the old flame.
sententiae.note: Dido confesses to her sister Anna that Aeneas has stirred the feelings she had for her dead husband Sychaeus. Dante has his pilgrim say the same words, in Italian, on seeing Beatrice again.

steps.explain: *vetus* is a third-declension adjective of one ending; *veteris* is genitive singular, with *flammae*.

options: A real fire in the palace
steps.explain: The flame of love is an old metaphor; Book 4 keeps returning to fire and wounds for Dido's love.
A vestige is a trace; to investigate is to follow the footprints. (Vest and vestry come from *vestis*, "clothing".)

sententiae.english: The gods thought otherwise.
sententiae.note: On the night Troy falls, the Trojan Rhipeus dies, "most just of all the Trojans". Aeneas can say only this: the gods saw it differently.

steps.explain: *dīs* is a short dative plural of *deus*. With *vīsum (est)*: "it seemed otherwise to the gods".
The perfect passive *vīsum est*, "it seemed", often drops *est* in verse.

steps.prompt: What is the tone of the line?
options: Resigned: justice did not save him
steps.explain: Three words, no complaint: the understatement makes the injustice felt.

sententiae.latin: Tū nē cēde malīs, sed contrā audentior ītō.
sententiae.english: Do not yield to troubles, but go against them the more boldly.
sententiae.note: The Sibyl foretells wars in Italy and another Achilles, yet tells Aeneas not to give way: the first road to safety, she says, will open from a Greek city.

steps.prompt: *nē cēde* is a negative command. Which is the usual prose form?
steps.explain: Prose says *nōlī* + infinitive; poets allow *nē* + the imperative.
Verbs of yielding take the dative.
*audēns* makes the comparative *audentior*: go "bolder", i.e. more boldly.

sententiae.latin: Fāma, malum quā nōn aliud vēlōcius ūllum.
sententiae.english: Rumor, an evil swifter than any other.
sententiae.note: The start of Vergil's portrait of Rumor as a monster, small at first, then striding the earth with her head in the clouds, spreading the news of Dido and Aeneas.

steps.latin: malum quā nōn aliud vēlōcius ūllum
steps.explain: After the comparative *vēlōcius*, the ablative *quā* means "than which": "an evil than which no other is swifter".
Comparatives end *-ius* in the neuter; it agrees with *aliud ... malum*.
Velocity is speed, from *vēlōx*, "swift".

sententiae.latin: Nōbīs, cum semel occidit brevis lūx, nox est perpetua ūna dormienda.
sententiae.english: For us, once our brief light has set, there is one endless night to be slept.
sententiae.note: The center of Catullus' kiss poem: suns can set and rise again, but a human life, once set, does not. Hence the thousand kisses.

steps.prompt: *est ... dormienda* is a passive periphrastic. What does it express?
steps.explain: The gerundive with *sum* says what has to happen: one night must be slept through.
With the passive periphrastic, the person who must do it goes in the dative: "a night must be slept by us".
Perpetual means unending; to perpetuate is to make last.

sententiae.latin: Atque in perpetuum, frāter, avē atque valē.
sententiae.english: And for ever, brother, hail and farewell.
sententiae.note: The last line of the poem Catullus wrote at his brother's grave near Troy, having traveled "through many peoples and many seas" to bring the last gifts.

steps.latin: Atque in perpetuum, frāter, avē atque valē.
options: Vocative: he speaks to his brother
steps.explain: Catullus addresses his dead brother directly; a third-declension vocative looks like the nominative.

steps.prompt: *avē* and *valē* are imperatives. What did Romans use them for?
steps.explain: *avē* ("be well") greeted, *valē* ("be strong") said goodbye. Joined here, they make meeting and parting a single moment.

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *valeō*, "be strong, be well"?
steps.explain: Valiant, valid and value all come from *valeō*. (Valley comes from *vallis*; veil from *vēlum*.)

sententiae.english: Let arms yield to the toga.
sententiae.source: Cicero, *On Duties* 1.77, quoting his own poem
sententiae.note: Cicero thought his defeat of Catiline's plot as consul, a civilian's victory, was worth any general's. The toga was the dress of peace and civic life.

options: Present subjunctive, used as a command: "let them yield"
steps.explain: Third-conjugation present subjunctive has *-a-*: *cēdat, cēdant*. Standing alone, it is jussive.
Metonymy: naming a thing by something closely linked to it. The toga stands for civil life.
Verbs of yielding take the dative of what is yielded to. *togae* could be genitive in form; the verb settles it.

sententiae.english: The strictest law is the greatest injustice.
sententiae.source: Cicero, *On Duties* 1.33, calling it a proverb already worn
sententiae.note: Law applied to the letter, without regard to fairness, becomes injustice. Cicero's example: a man who agreed a truce of thirty days and ravaged the fields by night, since the terms said days.

steps.explain: The adjective takes the gender of each noun: *iūs, iūris* (n.), *iniūria* (f.).

steps.prompt: *iūs* and *iniūria* share a root. What does the *in-* do?
steps.explain: *in-* before adjectives and nouns often means "not": *iniūria*, "not-right".

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *iūs, iūris*?
steps.explain: Jury, justice and injury come from *iūs*. (Journey comes from *diurnus*, "daily"; juggle from *ioculor*, "joke".)

sententiae.english: Practice is the best teacher.
sententiae.note: A saying Cicero uses in passing in a speech for a banker; it has outlived the case. In English, "practice makes perfect".

steps.explain: *ūsus* is the subject; *magister optimus* is what it is.

steps.prompt: *optimus* is the superlative of which adjective?
steps.explain: An irregular comparison: *bonus, melior, optimus*: good, better, best.
The genitive *-ūs* marks the fourth declension, like *manus, manūs*.

sententiae.english: Know yourself.
sententiae.source: the Latin form of the saying carved at Apollo's temple at Delphi
sententiae.note: Cicero says Apollo's command means "know your mind", since the body is only the mind's vessel (*Tusculan Disputations* 1.52).

steps.explain: Third-conjugation singular commands end in *-e*: *nōsce*, *lege*, *scrībe*. (A few are short: *dīc, dūc, fac, fer*.)
*ipse* intensifies: *tē ipsum*, "you yourself".
Notion, notice and notify come from *nōscō*; cognition and recognize from its compound *cognōscō*.

sententiae.english: Nothing can be created from nothing.
sententiae.note: Lucretius, a follower of Epicurus, argues that the world is made of atoms moving in the void, with no gods making things out of nothing. This is his first principle.

steps.prompt: Why the infinitive *posse*, with no main verb?
options: It is indirect statement: the poem reports a principle
steps.explain: In the poem the words depend on a verb of seeing: (when we see that) nothing can be created. Accusative *nīl*, infinitive *posse*.
First-conjugation passive infinitives end in *-ārī*.
Creature, create and recreation come from *creō*. (Creed comes from *crēdō*.)

sententiae.english: Hannibal is at the gates!
sententiae.source: a Roman cry of alarm, remembered for centuries
sententiae.note: Hannibal came within sight of Rome in 211 BC and never took it, but Romans went on using the cry for any danger close at hand. Cicero uses it in his speeches.

steps.explain: *ad* takes the accusative: "at the gates", right at the city.
A cry needs no verb: "Hannibal (is) at the gates!"
A portal is a gateway; a porter kept the gate. (Portrait comes from *trahō*, "draw"; pork from *porcus*.)

sententiae.english: From the egg to the apples.
sententiae.note: A Roman dinner began with eggs and ended with fruit, so this meant from start to finish. Horace uses it of a singer who won't sing when asked and, once started, won't stop.

steps.explain: *ab* takes the ablative.

steps.prompt: *māla* here means apples, not evils. What tells them apart?
steps.explain: Only vowel length separates them, which Roman punsters enjoyed.
Oval means egg-shaped. (An ovation comes from *ovō*, "rejoice".)

sententiae.english: Now we must drink.
sententiae.note: Horace celebrates the defeat of Cleopatra in 31 BC, then turns, in the same poem, to praise her courage in choosing death over being led in a Roman triumph.

steps.prompt: *bibendum est* is an impersonal passive periphrastic. It means...
options: "there must be drinking": we must drink
steps.explain: The gerundive with *est* and no subject says what must be done by everyone.

steps.prompt: What gives the line its urgency?
steps.explain: Putting "now" first makes the news the point: the celebration is due.
To imbibe is to drink in. (Bible comes from Greek *biblia*, "books".)

sententiae.latin: Ēheu fugācēs, Postume, Postume, lābuntur annī.
sententiae.english: Alas, Postumus, Postumus, the fleeting years slip by.
sententiae.note: Horace to a friend: no amount of piety delays wrinkles, old age or death. The doubled name sounds like a sigh.

steps.latin: Ēheu fugācēs, Postume, Postume, lābuntur annī.
steps.explain: Nominative plural masculine: "the fleeting years", adjective at the start of the line and noun at the end.

options: Feeling: the doubling sounds like a sigh
steps.explain: Doubling a word (geminatio) often marks emotion.

steps.prompt: *lābuntur* is deponent. What does it mean?
steps.explain: Deponents are passive in form, active in meaning. Don't confuse *lābor, lābī*, "slip", with *labor, labōris*, "work".

sententiae.english: Nothing is too steep for mortals.
sententiae.note: From a poem to the ship carrying Vergil to Greece: humans dare everything, crossing seas, stealing fire, flying like Daedalus. Horace means it as a warning, not a boast.

steps.explain: A partitive genitive after *nīl*: "nothing (of the) steep", i.e. nothing steep.
A dative of reference: nothing is steep for mortals.

steps.prompt: Is the line praise or warning?
options: A warning: people will try anything, and pay for it
steps.explain: The poem goes on: "we seek heaven itself in our folly".

sententiae.latin: Ūnus homō nōbīs cūnctandō restituit rem.
sententiae.english: One man, by delaying, restored the state for us.
sententiae.source: Ennius, *Annals*, quoted by Cicero (*On Old Age* 10)
sententiae.note: On Fabius Maximus, who would not meet Hannibal in open battle and wore him down instead. He was nicknamed *Cūnctātor*, the Delayer.

steps.latin: Ūnus homō nōbīs cūnctandō restituit rem.
options: A gerund in the ablative: "by delaying"
steps.explain: The gerund is a verbal noun; its ablative says how: "by delaying".
*rēs* on its own can stand for *rēs pūblica*, the Roman state.
Restitution is giving back what was lost. (Restaurant comes from *restaurō*, a different verb.)

sententiae.english: Man is a wolf to man.
sententiae.note: In the comedy a merchant won't hand money to a stranger: "man is a wolf to a man he doesn't know". Thomas Hobbes made the line famous.

steps.explain: The dative of *homō*: a wolf "to a man".

steps.prompt: *homō hominī* sets one word in two cases side by side. What is that called?
steps.explain: Polyptoton: the same word in different forms, pressed together to point the paradox.
Lupine means wolfish, from *lupus*.

sententiae.english: Whoever loves the golden mean…
sententiae.note: Whoever loves the golden middle way, Horace goes on, is safe both from a hovel's squalor and a palace's envy. English has called it "the golden mean" ever since.

steps.explain: Feminine accusative singular, wrapped round *quisquis* to reach its noun.
*quisquis* is an indefinite relative pronoun: "whoever".
An aureole is a golden halo; the chemical symbol Au is *aurum*. (Aura is Greek; aural comes from *auris*, "ear".)

sententiae.latin: Nōn quī parum habet, sed quī plūs cupit, pauper est.
sententiae.english: Not the one who has little, but the one who wants more, is poor.
sententiae.note: Seneca to Lucilius on wealth: it is not how much you have but how much you want that makes you poor.

steps.latin: Nōn quī parum habet, sed quī plūs cupit, pauper est.
options: *quī plūs cupit*: the one who wants more
steps.explain: *Nōn ... sed*: not the first relative clause, but the second. *pauper* is the predicate.
*multum, plūs, plūrimum*: much, more, most.
Poverty and pauper come from *pauper*; poor too, through French.

sententiae.english: While it is put off, life runs by.
sententiae.note: From Seneca's first letter: we lose most of life doing wrong, much of it doing nothing, and all of it by putting things off.

gloss.meaning: put off; differtur, is put off

steps.explain: *differō* is a compound of irregular *ferō*: passive *fertur*, *differtur*.

steps.prompt: What is the subject of both verbs?
steps.explain: Life is put off, and life runs past: one subject, held back until after *differtur*.
Differ and different come from *differō*, "carry apart". (Difficult comes from *difficilis*.)

sententiae.english: Muse, tell me the causes.
sententiae.note: The invocation of the Muse: why did Juno hate a man so good? Three lines later comes *tantaene animīs caelestibus īrae?*

options: Vocative: the poet calls on her
steps.explain: He speaks to the Muse. First-declension vocatives look like the nominative.
A first-conjugation singular command is the stem: *memorā*.
Memorial, memory and memorize.

sententiae.english: Each of us suffers his own spirit.
sententiae.note: Anchises on how souls are cleansed after death. What "his own *Mānēs*" means (one's own shade, fate or punishment) is still argued over.

steps.prompt: *quisque* is "each", but *patimur* is "we suffer". How do they fit?
options: Each of us: the plural verb takes everyone in
steps.explain: Latin allows "each" with a plural verb: "we each suffer".

steps.prompt: *patimur* is deponent. So its form is...
options: passive, but its meaning active: "we suffer"
steps.explain: Deponents have passive endings and active meanings.

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *patior, passus*?
steps.explain: Passion, patient and compassion come from *patior*. (Pass comes from *passus*, "step".)

sententiae.latin: Ībant obscūrī sōlā sub nocte per umbram.
sententiae.english: They went, dark, beneath the lonely night, through the shadow.
sententiae.note: Aeneas and the Sibyl enter the underworld. Vergil swaps the adjectives: it is the night that should be dark and the travelers who are alone.

steps.latin: Ībant obscūrī sōlā sub nocte per umbram.
steps.explain: *eō* has the imperfect *ībam, ībās, ībat, ībāmus, ībātis, ībant*.

steps.prompt: *obscūrī* describes the travelers, *sōlā* the night. What is this swap called?
steps.explain: Each adjective goes with the "wrong" noun, and the line feels the stranger for it.
*sub* takes the ablative for position, "beneath".

sententiae.latin: Dā mī bāsia mīlle, deinde centum.
sententiae.english: Give me a thousand kisses, then a hundred.
sententiae.note: The count goes on, another thousand, a second hundred, until they muddle the total so no one can cast the evil eye on so many kisses.

steps.latin: Dā mī bāsia mīlle, deinde centum.
steps.explain: *mī* is a contracted dative of *ego*, common in verse and speech.
Neuter plural *bāsia*, the object of *dā*.
A millennium is a thousand years; mile (*mīlle passūs*, a thousand paces) and million come from *mīlle* too.

sententiae.english: To whom do I give this charming new little book?
sententiae.note: The first line of Catullus' book. The answer: the historian Cornelius Nepos, who thought Catullus' "trifles" were worth something.

steps.explain: *cui* is the dative of *quis*.

steps.prompt: *libellus* is a diminutive of *liber*. What does *-ellus* add?
steps.explain: Diminutives can be modest and affectionate at once.
Novel, novice and renovate come from *novus*. (Naval comes from *nāvis*, "ship".)

sententiae.latin: Mulier cupidō quod dīcit amantī, in ventō et rapidā scrībere oportet aquā.
sententiae.english: What a woman says to an eager lover should be written on the wind and running water.
sententiae.note: Lesbia says she would marry no one but Catullus, not even Jupiter if he asked. "She says so," Catullus answers, and this is the rest.

steps.latin: Mulier cupidō quod dīcit amantī, in ventō et rapidā scrībere oportet aquā.
steps.explain: The relative clause, placed first, is the object: "what she says, one ought to write on wind and water".
*oportet* is impersonal: "it is fitting to write".

steps.prompt: What is Catullus saying about her promise?
options: It is a joke he enjoys
steps.explain: Words written on wind and flowing water vanish as they are written.

sententiae.latin: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa in partēs trēs.
sententiae.english: Gaul as a whole is divided into three parts.
sententiae.note: The first words of Caesar's account of his wars in Gaul, 58 to 50 BC: the Belgae, the Aquitani and the Celts, "whom we call Gauls". The course reads the chapter in Level III.

steps.latin: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa in partēs trēs.
options: A perfect passive used for a state: "is divided"
steps.explain: The perfect participle with *est* describes how Gaul now stands: divided.
*in* + accusative means "into".
Division, divide and individual. (Divine and diva come from *dīvus*, "godlike".)

sententiae.latin: Ferē libenter hominēs id quod volunt crēdunt.
sententiae.english: People generally believe what they want to believe.
sententiae.note: Caesar's officer Sabinus sends a spy to tell a Gallic army the Romans are about to flee. The Gauls believe it because they want to, attack, and are beaten.

steps.latin: Ferē libenter hominēs id quod volunt crēdunt.
steps.explain: *id quod volunt*: "that which they want".
Two verbs share *volō*: *volō, velle*, "want", and *volō, volāre*, "fly". *volunt* can only be "they want".
Credible, credit and creed come from *crēdō*.

sententiae.latin: Ō fortūnātam nātam mē cōnsule Rōmam!
sententiae.english: O fortunate Rome, born in my consulship!
sententiae.source: Cicero's poem on his own consulship, mocked by Juvenal (*Satires* 10.122)
sententiae.note: Cicero wrote an epic about his year as consul, 63 BC. Later writers quoted this line to laugh at it: the boast, and the jingle of *-nātam nātam*.

steps.latin: Ō fortūnātam nātam mē cōnsule Rōmam!
steps.explain: An exclamation can take the accusative: "O fortunate Rome!"

steps.prompt: *mē cōnsule* is an ablative absolute. It means...
options: "with me as consul": in my consulship
steps.explain: Two ablatives with "being" understood: *mē cōnsule*, "I being consul".

steps.prompt: Why did readers mock the line?
options: Its self-praise and its jingling sounds
steps.explain: Praising yourself for saving Rome, with *-nātam nātam* ringing like a bell.

sententiae.latin: Nihil est tam incrēdibile quod nōn dīcendō fīat probābile.
sententiae.english: Nothing is so unbelievable that speaking cannot make it believable.
sententiae.note: Cicero sets out to argue for the Stoics' strangest claims (only the wise are rich, all wrongs are equal) to show what oratory can do.

steps.latin: Nihil est tam incrēdibile quod nōn dīcendō fīat probābile.
options: A gerund in the ablative: "by speaking"
steps.explain: The ablative of the gerund says how: "by speaking".

options: After *tam*, *quod nōn* gives a result: "so unbelievable that it does not become..."
steps.explain: A relative clause of result (or characteristic): nothing is such that it cannot be made believable.
Probable, from *probō*, "test, approve". (The other three are Greek.)

sententiae.english: Time, devourer of things.
sententiae.note: Pythagoras again: time and envious old age destroy everything, gnawing slowly with their teeth.

steps.explain: With *edāx*, "devouring of things": the genitive of what is devoured.
Adjectives in *-āx* describe a tendency: *edāx* "greedy", *audāx* "bold", *fugāx* "fleeing".
Edible and inedible come from *edō*. (Edit comes from *ēdō*, "give out"; educate from *ēducō*.)

sententiae.latin: Omnium cōnsēnsū capāx imperiī, nisi imperāsset.
sententiae.english: By everyone's agreement fit to rule, had he not ruled.
sententiae.note: Tacitus on Galba, emperor for seven months in 69 AD: while a private citizen he seemed too great to be one, and all would have thought him fit for power, if he had never held it.

gloss.meaning: able to hold, fit for (with the genitive)

steps.latin: Omnium cōnsēnsū capāx imperiī, nisi imperāsset.
steps.explain: *-āvisse-* often contracts to *-āsse-*. The pluperfect subjunctive makes a past contrary-to-fact condition: "if he had not ruled".
Adjectives of ability take the genitive: "capable of rule".

options: The last words undo all the praise before them
steps.explain: A sententia with its sting in the tail: everything hangs on *nisi imperāsset*.

sententiae.english: Oh dear, I think I'm becoming a god.
sententiae.source: the emperor Vespasian, dying, as Suetonius reports (*Vespasian* 23)
sententiae.note: Emperors were declared gods after death. Vespasian, known for his dry wit, joked about it as he felt himself dying in 79 AD.

steps.explain: *fīō, fierī* serves as the passive of *faciō*: "be made, become".

options: It completes *fīō*: I become a god
steps.explain: Verbs of becoming, like *sum*, take a predicate nominative.

options: Emperors were made gods after death, so feeling divine meant dying
steps.explain: A deathbed joke at the expense of his own coming deification.

sententiae.english: Hail, Emperor, those about to die salute you.
sententiae.note: Suetonius reports it from men about to fight a staged sea battle for Claudius in 52 AD. Despite its fame, it was probably not a regular gladiators' greeting.

options: A future participle used as a noun: "those about to die"
steps.explain: The future participle ends *-ūrus*: *moritūrus*, "about to die".
The men address the emperor directly.
Salute, from *salūtō*, "wish health". (Salary comes from *sāl*, "salt".)

sententiae.latin: Audīrēs ululātūs fēminārum, īnfantum quirītātūs, clāmōrēs virōrum.
sententiae.english: You could have heard the shrieks of women, the wailing of children, the shouts of men.
sententiae.note: In the darkness, as ash falls on Misenum, Pliny and his mother join the crowds fleeing. The letter is on the AP syllabus and in the Reading Room.

gloss.meaning: hear; audīrēs, you could have heard

steps.prompt: *audīrēs* is an imperfect subjunctive standing alone. It means...
steps.latin: Audīrēs ululātūs fēminārum, īnfantum quirītātūs, clāmōrēs virōrum.
steps.explain: A potential subjunctive: what anyone there would have heard.

steps.prompt: Three noun phrases in a row. What is the figure?
steps.explain: A tricolon: three parallel members. The middle one swaps the order of genitive and noun, a small chiasmus inside it.
Infant, from *īnfāns*, "not yet speaking". (Infer comes from *ferō*; inform from *fōrma*.)

sententiae.latin: Iam nāvibus cinis incidēbat, quō propius accēderent, calidior et dēnsior.
sententiae.english: Already ash was falling on the ships, hotter and thicker the nearer they came.
sententiae.note: Pliny's uncle sails toward Vesuvius to bring help; ash, then pumice, falls on the ships. The letter is on the AP syllabus and in the Reading Room.

steps.explain: Compounds of *in-* often take the dative.
The comparative ends *-ior*; they describe *cinis*.
The imperfect paints action going on: ash falling and falling as they sail in.

sententiae.latin: Nōn amō tē, Sabidī, nec possum dīcere quārē.
sententiae.english: I don't like you, Sabidius, and I can't say why.
sententiae.note: The second line: *hoc tantum possum dīcere: nōn amō tē*, "this only I can say: I don't like you." An English schoolboy turned it into "I do not love thee, Dr. Fell".

steps.latin: Nōn amō tē, Sabidī, nec possum dīcere quārē.
steps.explain: Names in *-ius* have a vocative in *-ī*: *Sabidī*, like *fīlī*.
Here it is an indirect question with the verb left out: "(why I don't)".

options: He gives no reason, and the second line gives none again
steps.explain: The epigram circles back to its start, which is the point.

sententiae.english: He gives twice who gives quickly.
sententiae.note: Publilius wrote *inopī beneficium bis dat quī dat celeriter*, "he gives a kindness to the needy twice who gives it quickly". The short form is the proverb.

steps.prompt: What is the subject of the first *dat*?
steps.explain: The relative clause stands for its antecedent.
*citō* modifies the verb *dat*.
A biscuit is *bis coctus*, "twice cooked". Bicycle and binary take the same idea from *bi-*.

sententiae.english: The wickedness of the few is the disaster of the many.
sententiae.note: One of Publilius' lines that reads like a comment on Roman politics in the years of the civil wars, when it was written.

options: Genitive plural: "of the few", "of the many"
steps.explain: Each genitive goes with the noun beside it.

steps.prompt: The line sets few against many, wickedness against disaster. What figure?
steps.explain: Parallel halves with opposite ideas: antithesis. The rhyme *-tās ... -tās* sharpens it.
Calamity, a disaster. (Calamari comes from *calamus*, "pen", for the squid's shape.)

sententiae.english: The greatest respect is owed to a child.
sententiae.note: Juvenal on parents: children copy their elders' vices, so if you are about to do something shameful, remember the child who is watching.

steps.explain: Feminine nominative singular, first and last words of the line.
Respect is owed *to* the child.
Debt and debit come from *dēbeō*; the silent *b* is Latin showing through.

sententiae.latin: Ad rīvum eundem lupus et agnus vēnerant, sitī compulsī.
sententiae.english: A wolf and a lamb had come to the same stream, driven by thirst.
sententiae.note: The first fable of Phaedrus, a freedman of Augustus who put Aesop into Latin verse. The wolf finds one excuse after another to eat the lamb: the powerful do not need a reason.

steps.latin: Ad rīvum eundem lupus et agnus vēnerant, sitī compulsī.
steps.explain: The pluperfect adds *-erant* to the perfect stem *vēn-*.
*sitis* is an *i*-stem with ablative *sitī*: they were driven by thirst.

options: *lupus et agnus*, so it is plural
steps.explain: A participle describing two subjects together is plural.

sententiae.english: Out of many, one.
sententiae.source: the motto on the Great Seal of the United States (1782)
sententiae.note: Chosen for thirteen states made one nation. A poem once thought Vergil's, *Moretum*, uses almost the same words of a salad being mixed.

steps.explain: *ē/ex* takes the ablative.
The plural of the comparative *plūs*: "more", and so "many".

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *plūs, plūris*?
steps.explain: Plural, plus and surplus come from *plūs*.

sententiae.english: Almighty Jupiter, favor my bold undertaking.
sententiae.note: Ascanius prays before his first kill in battle (the scene of *sīc itur ad astra*). Adapted as *annuit coeptīs*, "he has favored our undertakings", it is on the back of the dollar bill.

options: Vocative: he prays to the god
steps.explain: Jupiter is addressed; his vocative looks like the nominative.
Verbs of favoring take the dative; *audācibus* agrees with it.
Omnipotent, all-powerful. (Ominous comes from *ōmen*; omission from *omittō*.)

sententiae.latin: Magnus ab integrō saeclōrum nāscitur ōrdō.
sententiae.english: The great order of the ages is born anew.
sententiae.note: A poem of 40 BC foretelling a golden age with the birth of a child. Christians later read it as a prophecy; the Great Seal of the United States adapts it as *novus ōrdō saeclōrum*.

steps.latin: Magnus ab integrō saeclōrum nāscitur ōrdō.
steps.explain: Adjective and noun frame the whole line.
Passive in form, active in sense: *nāscor*, "I am born".

steps.prompt: Which English word comes from *nāscor, nātus*?
steps.explain: Native, nation and nature come from *nāscor*. (Nasal comes from *nāsus*, "nose"; nausea from Greek.)

sententiae.english: I left in marble the city I received in brick.
sententiae.source: Augustus on Rome, as Suetonius reports (*Augustus* 28), in indirect speech
sententiae.note: Suetonius says Augustus boasted, with reason, that he had found Rome a city of brick and left it one of marble: he rebuilt temples, gave it a new forum, and paved it with public buildings.

steps.prompt: What noun is understood with *marmoream* and *latericiam*?
steps.explain: Feminine accusative singular: Rome, *urbs*.
Perfect stems with long vowels: *relīqu-*, *accēp-*.
To relinquish is to leave behind; relic, from *reliquiae*, "what is left", too.
